name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q01 - Matching crystalline and amorphous solid properties

questiontext.text:
Match the solids in List I with their characteristic structural or physical descriptions in List II.

List IList II
(A) Quartz(i) Photovoltaic material
(B) Quartz glass(ii) Long-range order and sharp melting point
(C) Polycrystalline metal(iii) Short-range order and isotropic
(D) Amorphous silicon(iv) Randomly oriented microcrystals

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Solids are classified as crystalline, amorphous, or polycrystalline based on the degree of order in the arrangement of their constituent particles.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Solid
Quartz is a crystalline solid with a three-dimensional repeating lattice, giving it long-range order and a sharp melting point.
Quartz glass is an amorphous solid (supercooled liquid) possessing only short-range order and isotropic physical properties.
Metals often exist as polycrystalline solids composed of randomly oriented microcrystals, making a bulk sample appear isotropic.
Amorphous silicon is one of the best photovoltaic materials available for converting sunlight into electricity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairing is: Quartz with long-range order and sharp melting point; Quartz glass with short-range order and isotropic; Polycrystalline metal with randomly oriented microcrystals; Amorphous silicon with photovoltaic material.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q02 - Matching crystalline solids with binding forces

questiontext.text:
Match the crystalline solids in List I with the primary attractive forces holding their constituent particles together in List II.

List IList II
(A) Solid \(\mathrm{I}_2\)(i) Coulombic or electrostatic forces
(B) Solid \(\mathrm{SO}_2\)(ii) Dispersion or London forces
(C) \(\mathrm{MgO}\)(iii) Covalent bonding
(D) \(\mathrm{SiC}\)(iv) Dipole-dipole interactions

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Crystalline solids are classified as molecular (non-polar, polar, hydrogen-bonded), ionic, metallic, or covalent/network solids depending on the binding forces between their constituent particles.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Solid
Solid \(\mathrm{I}_2\) consists of non-polar covalent molecules held together by weak dispersion or London forces.
Solid \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) consists of polar molecules held together by dipole-dipole interactions.
\(\mathrm{MgO}\) is an ionic solid made of \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{O}^{2-}\) ions bound by strong coulombic or electrostatic forces.
\(\mathrm{SiC}\) (silicon carbide) is a covalent or network solid in which atoms are linked throughout the crystal by directional covalent bonds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct correspondence is: Solid \(\mathrm{I}_2\) with dispersion or London forces; Solid \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) with dipole-dipole interactions; \(\mathrm{MgO}\) with coulombic or electrostatic forces; \(\mathrm{SiC}\) with covalent bonding.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q03 - Matching crystal systems with axial parameters

questiontext.text:
Match the crystal systems in List I with their corresponding axial distances and axial angles in List II.

List IList II
(A) Cubic(i) \(a = b \neq c;\ \alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90^\circ\)
(B) Tetragonal(ii) \(a \neq b \neq c;\ \alpha \neq \beta \neq \gamma \neq 90^\circ\)
(C) Hexagonal(iii) \(a = b = c;\ \alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90^\circ\)
(D) Triclinic(iv) \(a = b \neq c;\ \alpha = \beta = 90^\circ,\ \gamma = 120^\circ\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A three-dimensional unit cell is characterised by three edge lengths (\(a, b, c\)) and three interaxial angles (\(\alpha, eta, \gamma\)), which define the seven crystal systems.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Crystal System
In the cubic system, all three edges are equal and mutually perpendicular: \(a = b = c\) and \(\alpha = eta = \gamma = 90^\circ\).
In the tetragonal system, two edges are equal and all angles are \(90^\circ\): \(a = b eq c\) and \(\alpha = eta = \gamma = 90^\circ\).
In the hexagonal system, two edges are equal with \(\alpha = eta = 90^\circ\) and \(\gamma = 120^\circ\): \(a = b eq c\).
In the triclinic system, all edges and all angles are unequal and none of the angles equals \(90^\circ\): \(a eq b eq c\) and \(\alpha eq eta eq \gamma eq 90^\circ\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each crystal system with its axial parameters gives: Cubic with \(a = b = c,\ \alpha = eta = \gamma = 90^\circ\); Tetragonal with \(a = b eq c,\ \alpha = eta = \gamma = 90^\circ\); Hexagonal with \(a = b eq c,\ \alpha = eta = 90^\circ,\ \gamma = 120^\circ\); Triclinic with \(a eq b eq c,\ \alpha eq eta eq \gamma eq 90^\circ\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q04 - Matching crystal systems with Bravais lattice counts

questiontext.text:
Match the crystal systems in List I with the number and types of Bravais lattices possible in List II.

List IList II
(A) Orthorhombic(i) \(1\) (Primitive only)
(B) Monoclinic(ii) \(3\) (Primitive, Body-centred, Face-centred)
(C) Cubic(iii) \(4\) (Primitive, Body-centred, Face-centred, End-centred)
(D) Rhombohedral(iv) \(2\) (Primitive, End-centred)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bravais showed that there are \(14\) possible three-dimensional space lattices distributed across the seven crystal systems.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each System
The orthorhombic system exhibits all \(4\) variations: primitive, body-centred, face-centred, and end-centred.
The monoclinic system exhibits \(2\) variations: primitive and end-centred.
The cubic system exhibits \(3\) variations: primitive, body-centred, and face-centred.
The rhombohedral (trigonal) system exhibits only \(1\) variation: primitive.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, Orthorhombic corresponds to \(4\) variations, Monoclinic to \(2\), Cubic to \(3\), and Rhombohedral to \(1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q05 - Matching cubic unit cells with atom counts and packing efficiency

questiontext.text:
Match the crystal structures in List I with their effective number of atoms per unit cell (\(z\)) or coordination number and packing efficiency in List II.

List IList II
(A) Simple cubic(i) \(z = 4,\ 74\%\)
(B) Body-centred cubic (bcc)(ii) \(z = 1,\ 52.4\%\)
(C) Face-centred cubic (fcc)(iii) \(z = 2,\ 68\%\)
(D) Hexagonal close-packed (hcp)(iv) \(74\%\), coordination number \(12\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The effective number of atoms per cubic unit cell is found by summing the fractional contributions of corner, body-centre, and face-centre atoms, and packing efficiency is the percentage of total cell volume occupied by spheres.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Structure
In a simple cubic unit cell, \(z = 8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1\) and packing efficiency is \(52.4\%\).
In a body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell, \(z = 8 \times \frac{1}{8} + 1 = 2\) and packing efficiency is \(68\%\).
In a face-centred cubic (fcc/ccp) unit cell, \(z = 8 \times \frac{1}{8} + 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 4\) and packing efficiency is \(74\%\).
In a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure, each sphere touches \(12\) neighbours and \(74\%\) of the space is filled.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, Simple cubic matches \(z = 1,\ 52.4\%\); bcc matches \(z = 2,\ 68\%\); fcc matches \(z = 4,\ 74\%\); and hcp matches \(74\%\), coordination number \(12\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q06 - Matching point defects with ionic solid examples

questiontext.text:
Match the point defects in List I with their characteristic examples in List II.

List IList II
(A) Frenkel defect(i) \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) and \(\mathrm{KCl}\)
(B) Schottky defect(ii) \(\mathrm{AgBr}\)
(C) Both Frenkel and Schottky defects(iii) \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) doped with \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\)
(D) Impurity defect(iv) \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) and \(\mathrm{AgCl}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionic solids exhibit Frenkel and Schottky defects as stoichiometric point defects depending on relative ion sizes, and impurity defects when aliovalent ions are introduced.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Defect
Frenkel defect occurs when there is a large size difference between cation and anion, as in \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) and \(\mathrm{AgCl}\).
Schottky defect occurs when cation and anion have almost similar sizes, as in \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) and \(\mathrm{KCl}\).
\(\mathrm{AgBr}\) is a notable example that shows both Frenkel and Schottky defects.
Crystallising molten \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) containing a small amount of \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\) introduces \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ions and cationic vacancies, creating an impurity defect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, Frenkel defect pairs with \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) and \(\mathrm{AgCl}\); Schottky defect with \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) and \(\mathrm{KCl}\); Both Frenkel and Schottky defects with \(\mathrm{AgBr}\); and Impurity defect with \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) doped with \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q07 - Matching non stoichiometric defects with colours and formulas

questiontext.text:
Match the non-stoichiometric crystals in List I with their characteristic colour or defect feature in List II.

List IList II
(A) \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) heated in \(\mathrm{Na}\) vapour(i) Pink colour due to F-centres
(B) \(\mathrm{LiCl}\) with excess \(\mathrm{Li}\)(ii) Violet (lilac) colour due to F-centres
(C) \(\mathrm{KCl}\) with excess \(\mathrm{K}\)(iii) Yellow colour due to F-centres
(D) \(\mathrm{Fe}_{0.95}\mathrm{O}\)(iv) Metal deficiency defect with \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) ions

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Non-stoichiometric defects include metal excess defects (such as F-centres in alkali halides) and metal deficiency defects (such as variable-valence transition metal oxides).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Crystal
Heating \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) in sodium vapour produces anionic vacancies occupied by unpaired electrons (F-centres), imparting a yellow colour.
Excess lithium in \(\mathrm{LiCl}\) crystals imparts a pink colour.
Excess potassium in \(\mathrm{KCl}\) crystals imparts a violet (or lilac) colour.
\(\mathrm{Fe}_{0.95}\mathrm{O}\) exhibits a metal deficiency defect where some \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) ions are missing and electrical neutrality is maintained by \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) ions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) in \(\mathrm{Na}\) vapour with yellow colour; \(\mathrm{LiCl}\) with pink colour; \(\mathrm{KCl}\) with violet (lilac) colour; and \(\mathrm{Fe}_{0.95}\mathrm{O}\) with metal deficiency defect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q08 - Matching magnetic categories with examples

questiontext.text:
Match the magnetic properties in List I with the corresponding substance examples in List II.

List IList II
(A) Paramagnetic(i) \(\mathrm{MnO}\)
(B) Diamagnetic(ii) \(\mathrm{CrO}_2\)
(C) Ferromagnetic(iii) \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\)
(D) Antiferromagnetic(iv) \(\mathrm{O}_2\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Magnetic behaviour in solids depends on the presence of unpaired electrons and the alignment of magnetic moments of domains.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Category
\(\mathrm{O}_2\) contains unpaired electrons and is weakly attracted by a magnetic field, making it paramagnetic.
\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\) (benzene) has all electrons paired and is weakly repelled by a magnetic field, making it diamagnetic.
\(\mathrm{CrO}_2\) is strongly attracted by a magnetic field and can be permanently magnetised, making it ferromagnetic.
\(\mathrm{MnO}\) has equal numbers of oppositely oriented magnetic domains that cancel each other out, making it antiferromagnetic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, Paramagnetic matches \(\mathrm{O}_2\), Diamagnetic matches \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\), Ferromagnetic matches \(\mathrm{CrO}_2\), and Antiferromagnetic matches \(\mathrm{MnO}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q09 - Matching semiconductor materials and dopants

questiontext.text:
Match the semiconductor systems in List I with their correct classifications in List II.

List IList II
(A) \(\mathrm{Si}\) doped with \(\mathrm{As}\)(i) \(p\)-type semiconductor
(B) \(\mathrm{Ge}\) doped with \(\mathrm{In}\)(ii) Group \(12\text{–}16\) compound
(C) \(\mathrm{GaAs}\)(iii) \(n\)-type semiconductor
(D) \(\mathrm{CdSe}\)(iv) Group \(13\text{–}15\) compound

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Intrinsic group \(14\) semiconductors (\(\mathrm{Si}, \mathrm{Ge}\)) become \(n\)-type when doped with group \(15\) elements and \(p\)-type when doped with group \(13\) elements. Compound semiconductors are formed by combining group \(13\text{–}15\) or group \(12\text{–}16\) elements to simulate an average valence of four.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each System
\(\mathrm{As}\) belongs to group \(15\) (\(5\) valence electrons), so \(\mathrm{Si}\) doped with \(\mathrm{As}\) forms an \(n\)-type semiconductor.
\(\mathrm{In}\) belongs to group \(13\) (\(3\) valence electrons), so \(\mathrm{Ge}\) doped with \(\mathrm{In}\) creates electron holes and forms a \(p\)-type semiconductor.
\(\mathrm{GaAs}\) (gallium arsenide) is a group \(13\text{–}15\) compound semiconductor.
\(\mathrm{CdSe}\) is a group \(12\text{–}16\) compound semiconductor.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{Si}\) doped with \(\mathrm{As}\) pairs with \(n\)-type; \(\mathrm{Ge}\) doped with \(\mathrm{In}\) with \(p\)-type; \(\mathrm{GaAs}\) with group \(13\text{–}15\) compound; and \(\mathrm{CdSe}\) with group \(12\text{–}16\) compound.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q10 - Matching close packed layers with coordination numbers

questiontext.text:
Match the packing arrangements in List I with their coordination numbers in List II.

List IList II
(A) Close packing in one dimension(i) \(12\)
(B) Square close packing in two dimensions(ii) \(6\)
(C) Hexagonal close packing in two dimensions(iii) \(2\)
(D) Cubic close packing (ccp) in three dimensions(iv) \(4\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The coordination number of a sphere is the number of its nearest-neighbour spheres in direct contact.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Arrangement
In one-dimensional close packing, spheres are arranged in a single row, so each sphere touches \(2\) neighbours.
In two-dimensional square close packing (\(\text{AAA}\) type), each sphere touches \(4\) neighbours.
In two-dimensional hexagonal close packing (\(\text{ABAB}\) type), each sphere touches \(6\) neighbours.
In three-dimensional cubic close packing (ccp), each sphere touches \(12\) neighbours.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each arrangement to its coordination number gives: 1D close packing with \(2\); 2D square close packing with \(4\); 2D hexagonal close packing with \(6\); and 3D ccp with \(12\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q11 - Matching electrical conductivity ranges with solid classes

questiontext.text:
Match the types of solids in List I with their electrical conductivity ranges (in \(\Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\)) or metallic behaviour in List II.

List IList II
(A) Conductors(i) \(10^{-20}\) to \(10^{-10}\)
(B) Semiconductors(ii) \(10^{4}\) to \(10^{7}\)
(C) Insulators(iii) \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{4}\)
(D) Rhenium oxide (\(\mathrm{ReO}_3\))(iv) Copper-like conductivity and appearance

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Solids exhibit electrical conductivities spanning \(27\) orders of magnitude from \(10^{-20}\) to \(10^{7}\ \Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\) and are divided into conductors, semiconductors, and insulators.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Entry
Conductors have conductivities ranging from \(10^{4}\) to \(10^{7}\ \Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\).
Semiconductors have intermediate conductivities ranging from \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{4}\ \Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\).
Insulators have very low conductivities ranging from \(10^{-20}\) to \(10^{-10}\ \Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\).
Rhenium oxide (\(\mathrm{ReO}_3\)) is a transition metal oxide that behaves like metallic copper in its conductivity and appearance.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, Conductors match \(10^{4}\) to \(10^{7}\); Semiconductors match \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{4}\); Insulators match \(10^{-20}\) to \(10^{-10}\); and \(\mathrm{ReO}_3\) matches copper-like conductivity and appearance.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q12 - Matching unit cell edge and radius relations

questiontext.text:
Match the cubic unit cell features in List I with their corresponding edge-length relation or void count in List II.

List IList II
(A) Simple cubic(i) \(a = \frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\)
(B) Body-centred cubic (bcc)(ii) \(a = 2\sqrt{2}r\)
(C) Face-centred cubic (fcc)(iii) \(a = 2r\)
(D) Tetrahedral voids in one fcc unit cell(iv) \(8\) voids per unit cell

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
List I gives three cubic unit cells (simple cubic, bcc, fcc) and the tetrahedral voids in one fcc unit cell. List II gives edge-length to radius relations and void count.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Atoms are treated as identical hard spheres of radius \(r\) touching along the edge in simple cubic, along the body diagonal in bcc, and along the face diagonal in fcc.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Simple cubic: \(a = 2r\).
bcc: \(\sqrt{3}a = 4r \implies a = \frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\).
fcc: \(\sqrt{2}a = 4r \implies a = 2\sqrt{2}r\).
For \(N\) close-packed spheres, the number of tetrahedral voids is \(2N\); since an fcc unit cell has \(4\) atoms, it contains \(2 \times 4 = 8\) tetrahedral voids.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Matching each entry gives: Simple cubic \(\to a = 2r\); bcc \(\to a = \frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\); fcc \(\to a = 2\sqrt{2}r\); Tetrahedral voids in one fcc unit cell \(\to 8\) voids per unit cell.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All four pairs are dimensionally and conceptually verified. Thus, Simple cubic matches \(a = 2r\), bcc matches \(a = \frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\), fcc matches \(a = 2\sqrt{2}r\), and tetrahedral voids in one fcc unit cell matches \(8\) voids per unit cell.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q13 - Matching compound formulas from void occupancy

questiontext.text:
Anions \(\mathrm{B}\) form a close-packed lattice (ccp or hcp), while cations \(\mathrm{A}\) occupy the voids as described in List I. Match each occupancy condition in List I with the resulting chemical formula in List II.

List IList II
(A) \(\mathrm{A}\) occupies all octahedral voids(i) \(\mathrm{A}_4\mathrm{B}_3\)
(B) \(\mathrm{A}\) occupies \(\frac{1}{2}\) of octahedral voids(ii) \(\mathrm{A}_2\mathrm{B}_3\)
(C) \(\mathrm{A}\) occupies \(\frac{2}{3}\) of tetrahedral voids(iii) \(\mathrm{AB}\)
(D) \(\mathrm{A}\) occupies \(\frac{1}{3}\) of tetrahedral voids(iv) \(\mathrm{AB}_2\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Anions \(\mathrm{B}\) form a close-packed lattice of \(N\) spheres, and cations \(\mathrm{A}\) occupy specified fractions of octahedral or tetrahedral voids.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
For \(N\) close-packed spheres, the number of octahedral voids is \(N\) and the number of tetrahedral voids is \(2N\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The stoichiometric ratio \(\mathrm{A}:\mathrm{B}\) equals the ratio of the number of occupied voids to \(N\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. All octahedral voids occupied: \(\mathrm{A}:\mathrm{B} = N:N = 1:1 \implies \mathrm{AB}\).
2. Half of octahedral voids occupied: \(\mathrm{A}:\mathrm{B} = \frac{1}{2}N:N = 1:2 \implies \mathrm{AB}_2\).
3. Two-thirds of tetrahedral voids occupied: \(\mathrm{A}:\mathrm{B} = \left(\frac{2}{3} \times 2N\right):N = \frac{4}{3}:1 = 4:3 \implies \mathrm{A}_4\mathrm{B}_3\).
4. One-third of tetrahedral voids occupied: \(\mathrm{A}:\mathrm{B} = \left(\frac{1}{3} \times 2N\right):N = \frac{2}{3}:1 = 2:3 \implies \mathrm{A}_2\mathrm{B}_3\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All four ratios reduce to distinct simplest whole-number formulas: \(\mathrm{AB}\), \(\mathrm{AB}_2\), \(\mathrm{A}_4\mathrm{B}_3\), and \(\mathrm{A}_2\mathrm{B}_3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q14 - Matching lattice sites with unit cell contributions

questiontext.text:
Match the site of an atom or void in a cubic unit cell in List I with the fraction of it belonging to one particular unit cell in List II.

List IList II
(A) Atom at a corner(i) \(\frac{1}{2}\)
(B) Atom at a face centre(ii) \(\frac{1}{8}\)
(C) Octahedral void at an edge centre(iii) \(1\)
(D) Octahedral void at the body centre(iv) \(\frac{1}{4}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four positions in a cubic unit cell are given: corner, face centre, edge centre, and body centre.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The fraction belonging to a single unit cell equals \(\frac{1}{n}\), where \(n\) is the number of adjacent unit cells sharing that site.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
A corner is shared by \(8\) unit cells, a face centre by \(2\) unit cells, an edge centre by \(4\) unit cells, and the body centre by \(1\) unit cell (wholly inside).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Corner atom: shared among \(8\) cubes \(\implies \frac{1}{8}\).
2. Face-centre atom: shared between \(2\) cubes \(\implies \frac{1}{2}\).
3. Edge-centre octahedral void: shared among \(4\) cubes \(\implies \frac{1}{4}\).
4. Body-centre octahedral void: belongs entirely to \(1\) cube \(\implies 1\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Summing these in an fcc unit cell gives \(8 \times \frac{1}{8} + 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 4\) atoms and \(12 \times \frac{1}{4} + 1 = 4\) octahedral voids, confirming the fractions \(\frac{1}{8}, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, 1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q15 - Matching unit cell density and packing efficiency formulas

questiontext.text:
Match the cubic unit cell quantities in List I with their exact mathematical expressions in List II (where \(z\) is atoms per unit cell, \(M\) is molar mass, \(a\) is edge length, and \(N_A\) is Avogadro constant).

List IList II
(A) Density of cubic unit cell(i) \(\frac{\pi}{6} \times 100\%\)
(B) Packing efficiency of bcc(ii) \(\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}} \times 100\%\)
(C) Packing efficiency of ccp (fcc)(iii) \(\frac{zM}{a^3 N_A}\)
(D) Packing efficiency of simple cubic(iv) \(\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{8} \times 100\%\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
List I lists the density of a cubic unit cell and the packing efficiencies of bcc, ccp (fcc), and simple cubic lattices.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Each atom is a sphere of radius \(r\) with volume \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), and the cubic unit cell has volume \(a^3\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Density \(d = \frac{\text{mass of unit cell}}{\text{volume of unit cell}} = \frac{zM}{a^3 N_A}\).
Packing efficiency \(= \frac{z \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{a^3} \times 100\%\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. bcc (\(z = 2\), \(a = \frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\)):
\[\frac{2 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{\left(\frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^3} \times 100\% = \frac{\frac{8}{3}\pi}{\frac{64}{3\sqrt{3}}} \times 100\% = \frac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{8} \times 100\%\]
2. ccp/fcc (\(z = 4\), \(a = 2\sqrt{2}r\)):
\[\frac{4 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{(2\sqrt{2}r)^3} \times 100\% = \frac{\frac{16}{3}\pi}{16\sqrt{2}} \times 100\% = \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}} \times 100\%\]
3. Simple cubic (\(z = 1\), \(a = 2r\)):
\[\frac{1 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{(2r)^3} \times 100\% = \frac{\frac{4}{3}\pi}{8} \times 100\% = \frac{\pi}{6} \times 100\%\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Evaluating numerically gives \(\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{8} \approx 0.68\) (\(68\%\)), \(\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.74\) (\(74\%\)), and \(\frac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.524\) (\(52.4\%\)), confirming all four expressions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q16 - Matching covalent molecular and ionic solids with properties

questiontext.text:
Match the solids in List I with their characteristic structural or physical properties in List II.

List IList II
(A) Diamond(i) Hydrogen-bonded molecular solid, insulator
(B) Graphite(ii) Ionic solid showing Frenkel defect
(C) \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (ice)(iii) Soft layered solid, conductor and solid lubricant
(D) \(\mathrm{ZnS}\)(iv) Three-dimensional covalent network, very hard insulator

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The physical nature and electrical conductivity of solids are determined by their crystal structure and the type of bonding between constituent particles.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Solid
Diamond is a three-dimensional covalent network solid with strong directional bonds, making it very hard and an electrical insulator.
Graphite has carbon atoms arranged in layers where each atom is bonded to three neighbours and the fourth valence electron is mobile between layers; the layers can slide over one another, making graphite soft, a good solid lubricant, and an electrical conductor.
\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (ice) is a hydrogen-bonded molecular solid and an electrical insulator.
\(\mathrm{ZnS}\) is an ionic solid in which the large size difference between \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{S}^{2-}\) ions leads to Frenkel defects.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairing is: Diamond with three-dimensional covalent network, very hard insulator; Graphite with soft layered solid, conductor and solid lubricant; \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (ice) with hydrogen-bonded molecular solid, insulator; and \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) with ionic solid showing Frenkel defect.
